title: Sort files into folders by extension or by date
summary: Moves the files in a folder into subfolders named after their extension, such as jpg or txt. Another way is to sort by the year and month the file was last changed. Preview the moves first; a move never overwrites an existing file.

steps.explain: Preview only: print the mv command for each file that has a dot in its name. The folder name is the text after the last dot. Files with no dot, such as README, are not moved by this loop.
steps.cmd: (cd <DIR> && for f in *.*; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; printf 'mv -- %q %q\n' "$f" "${f##*.}/"; done)
steps.expect: Lines such as: mv -- x\ y.jpg jpg/

alternatives.explain: Preview sorting by the year and month of the last change. Nothing is moved.
alternatives.cmd: (cd <DIR> && for f in *; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; printf 'mv -- %q %q\n' "$f" "$(date -r "$f" +%Y/%m)/"; done)
alternatives.expect: Lines such as: mv -- a\ b 2023/07/

steps.explain: Move the files into the extension folders. Each folder is created when needed; mv -n leaves a file in place if the target name already exists.
steps.cmd: (cd <DIR> && for f in *.*; do [ -f "$f" ] || continue; d="${f##*.}"; mkdir -p -- "$d" && mv -n -- "$f" "$d/"; done)
steps.expect: No output. The loose files are now inside folders named after their extensions.

rollback.explain: Move the files back to the main folder. The preview output lists every move, so reverse each one.

warnings: Files are moved, so other programs that expect them in the old place will not find them.
JPG and jpg become two different folders on Linux, because names are case-sensitive.
Files with no dot in the name are not moved by the extension loop.
